title: Come, Lord Jesus (Revelation 22:6–21)
hook: the Bible ends with a prayer: even so, come, Lord Jesus

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tree of life by the river, its leaves for the healing of the nations. Your line was the healing of the nations. What small healing did you pass between two people? Day one thousand three hundred fifteen.

Two voices, one after the other, in the second-to-last verse of a Christian Bible. The one who testifies to these things says, in the King James words, "Surely I come quickly." And an answer comes straight back: "Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus." Then a single line of blessing, and the book is closed. After a garden, a flood, kings and exile, a cross and an empty tomb, beasts and a city of gold, the answer near the very end is one short word: come. Today's word is an even older way of saying it, kept in a language that isn't Greek at all.

First, the word. In the King James, maranatha turns up near the end of Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, left untranslated, in a hard line: "let him be Anathema Maranatha." Paul writes in Greek, but this word is Aramaic, and he doesn't stop to explain it, as if the church already knew it. Readers divide it two ways. Marana tha: our Lord, come. Or maran atha: our Lord has come. One is a plea, the other a statement, and the letters can carry both. The end of Revelation echoes the plea: come, Lord Jesus. Second, everyone is saying it. A few verses before the end: "And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come." The same word goes up to Christ and out to anyone thirsty. Come here; come to us. Third, quickly. "Surely I come quickly." Christians have read that quickly in different ways: soon in time, suddenly when it happens, or simply certain. The book doesn't stop to explain, and the church has kept saying come anyway. Fourth, where the word lives now. Paul tells the Corinthians that when they eat the bread and drink the cup, they "shew the Lord's death till he come." So the waiting is kept at a table. Some Christians say "come, Lord Jesus" in a grace before meals. Some churches sing maranatha in Advent, the weeks before Christmas. And then the very last verse of the Bible isn't a warning at all: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen."
screen: `THE SPIRIT AND THE BRIDE SAY COME.`
`KEPT AT A TABLE, ENDED IN GRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: if you pray, you can pray maranatha. Settle, and breathe. Let the old word ride on your breath in four even, unhurried syllables, ma-ra-na-tha, the way some Christian meditation groups say it. Slowly, for the length of the sit. When your mind wanders, come back to the word. If you don't pray, sit with the plain English word come, and notice what in your life you're waiting for: someone to arrive, something to mend, an ending to be good. Either way, don't hurry it. The bell holds the time.
Maranatha. An Aramaic word Paul left untranslated: our Lord, come, or our Lord has come. At the end of Revelation: even so, come, Lord Jesus.
Your line: come, lord jesus. Today, before one meal, pause for a breath and let the word come sit at the table with you, whatever you're waiting for. Day one thousand three hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Some Christians say 'come, Lord Jesus' in a grace before meals, and some churches sing or pray maranatha during Advent, the weeks of waiting before Christmas.

original.note: Aramaic, written in Greek letters in 1 Corinthians 16:22: "our Lord, come" (or, divided differently, "our Lord has come").

trapdoor: what you thought: the Bible ends with doom and a warning.
what it means: it ends with a short prayer, "even so, come, Lord Jesus", and then a blessing of grace.
what a scholar hears: maranatha, Aramaic kept inside Greek letters, divided marana tha (our Lord, come) or maran atha (our Lord has come).

notes: Maranatha is called Aramaic, with two divisions (marana tha / maran atha); this is a language claim from standard lexicons, not from the cited text. Confirm.

Editor: cut the uncited count 'only once' for maranatha in the King James; replaced the superlative 'one of the last things said on a human tongue' and the screen 'the last human word' with 'the answer near the very end'; varied the hook opening so it no longer echoes day 1314's 'turn to the last chapter'; fixed the unclear line 'sounds like the first'.

'Second-to-last verse' and 'one of the last things said on a human tongue' refer to Revelation 22:20–21 in the Christian ordering. The speaker of 'Amen. Even so, come' is not named in the text; the lesson says 'an answer comes back'.
Readings of 'quickly' (soon; sudden; certain) given unranked. Confirm.
The practice splits the word 'mara / natha' only as a breathing aid; confirm it is acceptable and not seen as a new prayer.
Original: μαράνα θά as printed in critical Greek texts of 1 Corinthians 16:22; some editions print μαρανα θα or μαραναθα. Confirm.

Audit 2026-10-02: maranatha is 'near the end' of 1 Corinthians (16:22, two verses before the close), not 'the very end'; the practice's 'mara / natha' split matched neither scholarly division, so it now uses the four syllables ma-ra-na-tha as some Christian meditation groups (e.g. John Main's) say it. Confirm.
